description: Soy un participante de 17 años apasionado por el espacio, la programación y la inteligencia artificial aplicada a las ciencias de la Tierra(y el espacio ). Aprendo de forma autodidacta y transformo datos abiertos en herramientas visuales útiles. En ROKO participo de forma individual analizando tendencias climáticas con datos oficiales de NASA POWER. Equipo cerrado, enfocado en la entrega del proyecto.
summary:
Mangarita is an interactive, lightweight climate explorer built in Python that makes real satellite and weather data from the NASA POWER API easy for anyone to understand and use.
Instead of forcing users to navigate complex scientific portals, Mangarita turns six key atmospheric and solar variables into clear visual comparisons, statistical trend checks, and mathematical future projections. A core feature of the app is its resilient local reserve: every queried location is saved on disk, so if internet access drops or NASA's servers are unreachable, Mangarita never invents numbers—it automatically finds the nearest verified location using geographic distance.
This matters because communities, students, and local planners—especially in regions with unstable internet—need trustworthy, easy-to-read climate data to make informed decisions. Mangarita bridges the gap between open NASA Earth science and everyday users, working reliably both online and completely offline.
details:
What it does and how it works
Mangarita is a lightweight, browser-based climate explorer built as a
single-file Python application. When launched, it loads a local reserve of real
monthly meteorological data from the NASA
POWER API (from 2021 to the present
across 75+ cities) and opens an interactive dashboard. Users can compare
contrasting global climates or search any coordinate on Earth to visualize six
key variables: temperature (T2M), relative humidity (RH2M), wind speed (WS10M), surface pressure (PS), precipitation (PRECTOTCORR), and solar radiation (ALLSKY_SFC_SW_DWN).

Benefits and
intended impact
Complex scientific portals are hard to use
for non-specialists or people with unstable internet. Mangarita makes NASA
Earth data accessible to students, farmers, and local communities. Every
queried location is cached in reserva_nasa.json; if internet access drops or the API fails, the
app never invents numbers—it uses the Haversine
formula to show the nearest
verified station saved on disk.

Tools and
technologies used

·         Backend
& Math: Python 3, requests (NASA POWER API), pandas, numpy (Student's t-test and least-squares harmonic
projections), and Python's built-in http.server.

·         Frontend: HTML5, CSS3, vanilla JavaScript (for offline
36-month projections), and Plotly for interactive dark-mode charts.

·         Development
Support: AI coding models assisted
with code structure, debugging, and documentation.

Creativity and
design considerations
I wanted climate science to feel
approachable yet honest. Mangarita features a friendly animated mascot
alongside strict scientific guardrails: physical limits (keeping humidity
between 0% and 100%), unit conversions (to W/m²), and widening 95% confidence
bands with clear disclaimers that mathematical trends are not weather forecasts.
